law: Knowledge Once — runtime and data substance defined here once, projected everywhere.

RUN.concepts: The Runtime Constitution defines how derived reality executes. Constitution defines truth; Domains manage truth; Runtime derives reality; Agents execute reality; Applications consume reality. The runtime never owns truth — it computes projections of it.
RUN.ontology: Runtime is a pure function over registry state. Inputs: primitives + registry. Outputs: projections. Side effects: only governed, evidenced actions. The runtime is stateless with respect to truth.
RUN.taxonomy: By layer: Projection / Orchestration / Execution / Interaction. By mode: Interactive / Batch / Streaming / Event-driven. By ownership: Platform / Tenant / Edge.
RUN.dataModel:
```yaml
RuntimeSession:
  sessionId: <Identity>
  inputs: {primitives: [<ref>], registryVersion: <version>}
  projections: [<content-addressed ref>]
  actions: [<governed action ref>]
  temporal: {startedAt, endedAt}
  context: <Context>
  evidence: [<Evidence>]
```
RUN.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Opening
    Opening --> Resolving
    Resolving --> Projecting
    Projecting --> Acting
    Acting --> Closing
    Closing --> [*]
```
workflow: open session with registry version → resolve context → compute projections → execute governed actions → close with full evidence
authorities: Runtime Authority (execution); every action carries the acting domain's delegated authority.
RUN.privacy: Sessions over personal data are consent-scoped and retention-bounded by policy.
RUN.audit: Every session is a complete audit artifact — inputs, registry version, projections, actions, and evidence form an unbroken chain.
RUN.twin: Runtime twin monitors projection latency and violation rates as platform health.
RUN.agent: Agents execute within the runtime; their actions are governed at the same enforcement points as everything else.
RUN.runtime: The runtime is deliberately stateless about truth — all truth is re-derived from the registry per session, guaranteeing consistency.
RUN.scaling: Sessions are independent and horizontally scalable; registry version pinning makes projections reproducible at any scale.
RUN.multiTenant: Sessions are tenant-isolated; cross-tenant projection requires published relationship and both authorities.
RUN.geo: Sessions run in-jurisdiction for regulated data; registry versions replicate for local resolution.
RUN.failure: Registry version skew, projection timeout, evidence gap mid-session, policy version race.
RUN.recovery: Sessions are replayable from registry state — a failed session re-derives identically. In-flight actions are idempotent.
RUN.certification: Runtime must prove every output is a deterministic function of registry state — no hidden state, no bypass paths.
RUN.migration: Runtime evolves by registry version; old sessions remain reproducible at their pinned version.
RUN.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller
    participant RT as Runtime
    participant RG as Registry
    C->>RT: open session
    RT->>RG: pin registry version
    RG-->>RT: version
    RT->>RT: project + act under governance
    RT-->>C: projections + evidence
```
RUN.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> VersionPinning
    VersionPinning --> ContextResolving
    ContextResolving --> Projecting
    Projecting --> Executing
```
RUN.blueprint: Build order for RUN: (1) define registry entries — this domain owns by layer: projection / orchestration / execution / interaction as registry truth, not code; (2) implement the contract surface first (runtime.session.open, runtime.project, runtime.act) and validate against RUN boundaries; (3) event-source all state so history is reconstructable; (4) wire the enforcement points — authority check, policy guard, evidence binding, trace — in-line, with no bypass path; (5) add tests per the Testing Architecture, citing evidence per gate; (6) obtain Verification and Certification before activation. Acceptance: the Zero Partial and Law 001 audits pass, every action answers the seven explainability questions, and this domain mutates no other domain internals.

RUN2.concepts: Execution Architecture defines how a single governed action runs. Every action passes authority check, policy guard, evidence binding, and trace recording — in that order, with no bypass.
RUN2.ontology: Execution is a pipeline: Authorize → Guard → Execute → Evidence → Trace. Each stage is mandatory and independently verifiable. A skipped stage is a constitutional violation.
RUN2.taxonomy: By synchronicity: Synchronous / Asynchronous / Deferred. By isolation: Shared / Isolated / Enclave. By idempotency: Idempotent / At-most-once / Compensatable.
RUN2.dataModel:
```yaml
Execution:
  executionId: <Identity>
  actionClass: <registry id>
  authority: <Authority>
  policyVersion: <version>
  input: <content-addressed>
  output: <content-addressed>
  evidence: [<Evidence>]
  trace: <append-only ref>
  temporal: {at}
  idempotencyKey: <hash>
```
RUN2.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Requested
    Requested --> Authorized
    Authorized --> Guarded
    Guarded --> Executed
    Executed --> Evidenced
    Evidenced --> Traced
    Traced --> [*]
    Guarded --> Denied
    Denied --> [*]
```
workflow: authorize (authority chain) → guard (policy evaluation) → execute (isolated) → bind evidence → append trace
authorities: The action class's owning authority; verified, never assumed.
RUN2.privacy: Traces minimize personal data; the enforcement facts are retained, subject contents are not.
RUN2.audit: The trace is the audit — every stage is a signed, timestamped, append-only entry. Replay reproduces identical outcome.
RUN2.twin: Execution twin monitors pipeline latency and denial rates as governance health.
RUN2.agent: Agent actions run through the identical pipeline — agents get no shortcut, by constitutional design.
RUN2.runtime: The pipeline is in-process for latency, with each stage writing to an append-only log before the next begins.
RUN2.scaling: Executions are independent; the append-only trace is the serialization point and is sharded by execution id.
RUN2.multiTenant: Executions are tenant-isolated; cross-tenant action classes require both authorities.
RUN2.geo: Execution locality follows data residency; traces stay in-jurisdiction.
RUN2.failure: Stage skip (must be impossible), evidence failure post-execution, trace write failure, idempotency collision.
RUN2.recovery: Failed executions compensate via recorded compensating actions — the pipeline is never left half-executed by design.
RUN2.certification: Pipeline completeness must be formally provable — a bypass path voids certification of the entire platform.
RUN2.migration: New action classes are registry additions; the pipeline schema is frozen.
RUN2.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller
    participant EX as Execution
    participant AU as Authority
    participant PL as Policy
    C->>EX: run(action, input)
    EX->>AU: authorize
    AU-->>EX: ok
    EX->>PL: guard
    PL-->>EX: permit
    EX->>EX: execute + evidence + trace
    EX-->>C: result
```
RUN2.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Authorizing
    Authorizing --> Guarding
    Guarding --> Executing
    Executing --> Evidencing
    Evidencing --> Tracing
```
RUN2.blueprint: Build order for RUN2: (1) define registry entries — this domain owns by synchronicity: synchronous / asynchronous / deferred as registry truth, not code; (2) implement the contract surface first (execution.run, execution.compensate, execution.replay) and validate against RUN2 boundaries; (3) event-source all state so history is reconstructable; (4) wire the enforcement points — authority check, policy guard, evidence binding, trace — in-line, with no bypass path; (5) add tests per the Testing Architecture, citing evidence per gate; (6) obtain Verification and Certification before activation. Acceptance: the Zero Partial and Law 001 audits pass, every action answers the seven explainability questions, and this domain mutates no other domain internals.

RUN3.concepts: Orchestration coordinates multiple governed executions into coherent outcomes without introducing a coordination truth of its own. The orchestrator holds no state — it holds a plan, and the plan is itself a governed projection.
RUN3.ontology: Orchestration has a Plan (workflow projection), Steps (executions), Dependencies (registry expressions), and Compensation logic. Sagas are first-class; distributed transactions across domains are prohibited (they'd create shared mutable truth).
RUN3.taxonomy: By pattern: Saga / Pipeline / Fan-out-fan-in / Stateful-coordination / Event-choreography. By duration: Request-scale / Minutes / Hours / Days. By failure mode: Compensatable / Retryable / Escalating.
RUN3.dataModel:
```yaml
Orchestration:
  orchestrationId: <Identity>
  plan: <workflow projection ref>
  steps: [{executionRef, dependsOn}]
  compensationPlan: [{step, compensatingAction}]
  state: <registry state>
  context: <Context>
  temporal: {startedAt}
```
RUN3.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Planned
    Planned --> Running
    Running --> StepOk
    StepOk --> Running
    Running --> StepFailed
    StepFailed --> Compensating
    Compensating --> Compensated
    Compensating --> Escalated: compensation fails
    Running --> Completed
    Completed --> [*]
    Compensated --> [*]
```
workflow: materialize plan → execute steps per dependency → on failure: compensate in reverse → escalate if compensation fails
authorities: Orchestration Authority (coordination); each step carries its own action-class authority.
RUN3.privacy: Orchestration over personal data inherits the strictest consent scope among its steps.
RUN3.audit: Every step and compensation is traced; the orchestration is replayable end-to-end from the plan + step traces.
RUN3.twin: Orchestration twin tracks in-flight plans and predicts failure cascades before compensation is needed.
RUN3.agent: Planner agents materialize plans; orchestration executes them — planning and execution are separated by constitution.
RUN3.runtime: Sagas with explicit compensation; no two-phase commit across domains — eventual consistency within a context window.
RUN3.scaling: Orchestrations are independent; long-running plans checkpoint to the event store and resume.
RUN3.multiTenant: Orchestration never crosses tenants; marketplace flows are explicit multi-party plans with both authorities.
RUN3.geo: Cross-region orchestration respects sovereignty — a step touching regulated data runs in-jurisdiction.
RUN3.failure: Step failure cascade, compensation failure, plan version drift, orphaned orchestration.
RUN3.recovery: Compensation is the recovery mechanism; escalation routes to governance. Orphaned plans are reaped by policy.
RUN3.certification: Plan must be compensatable — non-compensatable distributed steps are uncertifiable.
RUN3.migration: New patterns are registry additions to the workflow registry.
RUN3.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Coordinator
    participant OR as Orchestration
    participant E1 as Step 1
    participant E2 as Step 2
    C->>OR: start(plan)
    OR->>E1: execute
    E1-->>OR: ok
    OR->>E2: execute
    E2-->>OR: failed
    OR->>E1: compensate
    OR-->>C: compensated
```
RUN3.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Planning
    Planning --> Executing
    Executing --> Checkpointing
    Checkpointing --> Executing
    Checkpointing --> Completing
```
RUN3.blueprint: Build order for RUN3: (1) define registry entries — this domain owns by pattern: saga / pipeline / fan-out-fan-in / stateful-coordination / event-choreography as registry truth, not code; (2) implement the contract surface first (orchestration.start, orchestration.compensate, orchestration.suspend) and validate against RUN3 boundaries; (3) event-source all state so history is reconstructable; (4) wire the enforcement points — authority check, policy guard, evidence binding, trace — in-line, with no bypass path; (5) add tests per the Testing Architecture, citing evidence per gate; (6) obtain Verification and Certification before activation. Acceptance: the Zero Partial and Law 001 audits pass, every action answers the seven explainability questions, and this domain mutates no other domain internals.

RUN4.concepts: Workflow Architecture defines process orchestration as a governed, registry-defined projection. Workflows are not code — they are declarations in the workflow registry, executed by the orchestration engine.
RUN4.ontology: Workflow has Steps (action classes), Transitions (registry expressions), Guards (policies), and a state machine. Defining a workflow is a registry act, not a deployment act.
RUN4.taxonomy: By structure: Sequential / Branching / Parallel / Loop / Event-driven / Hybrid. By mutability: Frozen-versioned / Governed-evolving. By scope: Universal / Domain / Tenant / Instance.
RUN4.dataModel:
```yaml
Workflow:
  workflowId: <registry id>
  version: <int>
  steps: [{actionClass, guards: [Policy]}]
  transitions: [{from, to, condition}]
  stateMachine: <registry ref>
  compensationPlan: [{step, compensatingAction}]
  temporal: {effectiveFrom, effectiveTo}
```
RUN4.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Defined
    Defined --> Validated
    Validated --> Active
    Active --> Retired
    Retired --> [*]
```
workflow: define in registry → static validation (guards, compensatability, state machine sanity) → activate → instantiate per execution
authorities: Workflow Authority (registry governance); step authorities are inherited from action classes.
RUN4.privacy: Workflows over personal data carry consent scope as a first-class guard, not an afterthought.
RUN4.audit: Every instantiation records the workflow version — history is replayable because the version is immutable.
RUN4.twin: Workflow twin tracks execution distributions and bottleneck steps across instances.
RUN4.agent: Agents may define workflow proposals, but only the Workflow Authority activates them.
RUN4.runtime: Workflow is data interpreted by the orchestration engine — the engine has zero workflow-specific code.
RUN4.scaling: Definitions are few and globally cached; instances scale with orchestration.
RUN4.multiTenant: Universal workflows are shared; tenant workflows are registry entries scoped to the tenant.
RUN4.geo: Workflow guards include jurisdiction policy — the same workflow may be legal in one region, blocked in another.
RUN4.failure: Invalid guard reference, uncompensatable step, transition deadlock, version retirement with live instances.
RUN4.recovery: Versions are immutable; retirement prevents new instances, and live ones complete on their pinned version.
RUN4.certification: Workflow must pass static validation: guard completeness, state-machine reachability, and compensatability.
RUN4.migration: Workflow evolution is versioned registry evolution — there is no separate migration path.
RUN4.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant D as Definer
    participant WF as Workflow Registry
    participant EN as Engine
    D->>WF: define(steps, guards)
    WF->>WF: static validation
    WF-->>D: WorkflowDefined
    EN->>WF: load version
    WF-->>EN: definition
    EN->>EN: instantiate
```
RUN4.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Defining
    Defining --> Validating
    Validating --> Activating
    Activating --> Instantiating
```
RUN4.blueprint: Build order for RUN4: (1) define registry entries — this domain owns by structure: sequential / branching / parallel / loop / event-driven / hybrid as registry truth, not code; (2) implement the contract surface first (workflow.define, workflow.validate, workflow.version.retire) and validate against RUN4 boundaries; (3) event-source all state so history is reconstructable; (4) wire the enforcement points — authority check, policy guard, evidence binding, trace — in-line, with no bypass path; (5) add tests per the Testing Architecture, citing evidence per gate; (6) obtain Verification and Certification before activation. Acceptance: the Zero Partial and Law 001 audits pass, every action answers the seven explainability questions, and this domain mutates no other domain internals.

RUN5.concepts: State Machine Architecture makes lifecycle explicit and governed. Every stateful primitive and projection carries a registry-defined state machine; transitions are policy-guarded decisions, never silent mutations.
RUN5.ontology: StateMachine has States (registry), Transitions (guarded), Events (triggers), and Invariants (must-hold per state). The current state is a projection of the transition history — never stored independently.
RUN5.taxonomy: By determinism: Deterministic / Non-deterministic-governed. By persistence: Ephemeral / Persistent / Eternal. By complexity: Flat / Nested / Hierarchical / Orthogonal.
RUN5.dataModel:
```yaml
StateMachine:
  machineId: <registry id>
  states: [<registry state>]
  initialState: <registry state>
  transitions: [{from, to, event, guard: [Policy], action}]
  invariants: [{state, mustHold}]
  version: <int>
```
RUN5.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Idle
    Idle --> Evaluating: event
    Evaluating --> Guarding
    Guarding --> Occurred: permitted
    Guarding --> Denied: prohibited
    Occurred --> Idle
    Denied --> Idle
```
workflow: event arrives → resolve machine version → evaluate guard → apply transition → verify invariant → append to history
authorities: Machine Authority (definition); transitions carry the action class's authority.
RUN5.privacy: States over personal subjects are sensitive; transition history minimizes subject data.
RUN5.audit: State is derived from transition history — the history IS the audit; a stored state contradicting history is a violation.
RUN5.twin: State twin monitors machines for stuck states and transition hotspots.
RUN5.agent: Agents may propose transitions; guards decide — agents never bypass the machine.
RUN5.runtime: Evaluation is a function of (machine version, current state, event, guard result); idempotent by event key.
RUN5.scaling: Machines are per-subject and independent; history is append-only and sharded by subject.
RUN5.multiTenant: Machine definitions are shared or tenant-scoped via the registry; instances never cross tenants.
RUN5.geo: Guards include jurisdiction policy; a transition legal in one region may be denied in another.
RUN5.failure: Invariant violation post-transition, non-deterministic guard, history/state divergence, orphaned machine.
RUN5.recovery: Rebuild state by replaying history; rollback is a compensating transition recorded like any other.
RUN5.certification: Machine must pass reachability analysis, guard determinism, and invariant coverage.
RUN5.migration: Machines version in the registry; instances finish on their pinned version.
RUN5.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant E as Event
    participant SM as State Machine
    participant PL as Policy
    E->>SM: transition(subject, event)
    SM->>SM: load history → current state
    SM->>PL: evaluate guard
    PL-->>SM: permit/deny
    SM->>SM: append transition or deny
    SM-->>E: outcome
```
RUN5.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Loading
    Loading --> Resolving
    Resolving --> Guarding
    Guarding --> Appending
```
RUN5.blueprint: Build order for RUN5: (1) define registry entries — this domain owns by determinism: deterministic / non-deterministic-governed as registry truth, not code; (2) implement the contract surface first (stateMachine.define, stateMachine.transition, stateMachine.rollback) and validate against RUN5 boundaries; (3) event-source all state so history is reconstructable; (4) wire the enforcement points — authority check, policy guard, evidence binding, trace — in-line, with no bypass path; (5) add tests per the Testing Architecture, citing evidence per gate; (6) obtain Verification and Certification before activation. Acceptance: the Zero Partial and Law 001 audits pass, every action answers the seven explainability questions, and this domain mutates no other domain internals.

DB.concepts: Storage Architecture holds primitives and registry truth — nothing else. Commerce objects, products, offers, and projections are never stored; they are computed. The store is the memory of the constitution, not the memory of the business.
DB.ontology: Storage is partitioned by domain ownership: each domain owns its tables/shards exclusively. Cross-domain access is via contract, never via shared table. Append-only for truth; projections are cached, not stored.
DB.taxonomy: By truth: Authoritative (primitive/registry) / Derived (projection cache) / Ephemeral (session). By shape: Relational / Document / Graph / Blob / Time-series. By tier: Hot / Warm / Cold / Archive.
DB.dataModel:
```yaml
StoragePartition:
  partitionId: <Identity>
  ownerDomain: <Domain>
  storeType: <registry id>
  tier: <Hot|Warm|Cold|Archive>
  residency: <Context jurisdiction>
  retentionPolicy: <Policy>
  encryptionState: <registry id>
```
DB.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Provisioned
    Provisioned --> Active
    Active --> TiredDown
    TiredDown --> Archived
    Archived --> Purged
    Purged --> [*]
```
workflow: provision under domain ownership → write primitives only → tier by access pattern → archive per retention → purge under governance
authorities: Domain Authority owns its partitions; Storage Authority governs infrastructure policy.
permissions: storage.write (domain, to its own partition only)
DB.privacy: Retention and purge are policy-driven per data class; erasure requests execute as governed purges with certificates.
DB.audit: Every tier move, archive, and purge is recorded; storage operations are as audited as business actions.
DB.twin: Storage twin monitors capacity, tier efficacy, and purge backlog as platform health.
DB.agent: Storage agent proposes tiering and retention adjustments from access patterns, under governance.
DB.runtime: Writes are domain-scoped and schema-validated against the registry; reads route by domain contract.
DB.scaling: Partitions scale independently per domain — no global bottleneck, no cross-domain coupling.
DB.multiTenant: Tenant data isolation at the partition level; shared infrastructure never implies shared data.
DB.geo: Residency is a partition property — regulated data's partition physically resides in-jurisdiction.
DB.failure: Cross-domain write attempt (must be rejected), residency violation, retention policy conflict, tier thrash.
DB.recovery: Authoritative truth is append-only and replicated; projection caches are disposable and re-derived.
DB.certification: Partition must pass ownership binding, residency compliance, encryption state, and retention policy.
DB.migration: Storage engines are pluggable via the registry; migrating engines never touches domain logic.
DB.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant D as Domain
    participant ST as Storage
    participant PL as Policy
    D->>ST: write primitive
    ST->>ST: verify domain ownership
    ST->>PL: retention + residency check
    PL-->>ST: ok
    ST->>ST: append
    ST-->>D: ack
```
DB.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Owning
    Owning --> Validating
    Validating --> Appending
    Appending --> Replicating
```

Acceptance: the Zero Partial and Law 001 audits pass, every action answers the seven explainability questions, and this domain mutates no other domain internals.

GRF.concepts: Graph Architecture is the native shape of the platform — reality emerges through relationships. The graph stores primitives and their relationships; everything queryable about reality is a traversal.
GRF.ontology: Graph has Nodes (primitives/projections) and Edges (typed, contextualized, temporal). Traversal is context-filtered and trust-weighted. The graph is the substrate for Relationship, Causality, Discovery, and Emergence.
GRF.taxonomy: By content: Primitive-graph / Projection-graph / Meta-graph. By traversal: Local / Multi-hop / Global-pattern. By store: Native-graph / Relational-emulated / Distributed.
GRF.dataModel:
```yaml
GraphPartition:
  partitionId: <Identity>
  shardKey: <registry expression>
  nodes: <count>
  edges: <count>
  traversalPolicy: <Policy>
  residency: <Context>
  version: <int>
```
GRF.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Planning
    Planning --> Traversing
    Traversing --> Filtering
    Filtering --> Returning
```
workflow: parse query → plan traversal under policy → execute with context filter → trust-weight results → return
authorities: Graph Authority (infrastructure); traversal policy enforces each domain's access contract.
GRF.privacy: Sensitive edges are filtered at traversal — never returned then hidden. Hidden-edge traversal attempts are logged.
GRF.audit: Every traversal records the query, context, policies applied, and edge count — the basis of data-access audit.
GRF.twin: Graph twin monitors degree distribution and hotspot formation as structural health.
GRF.agent: Discovery agents traverse for inference; every traversal is policy-checked like any other access.
GRF.runtime: Traversal is bounded by policy hop-limit and trust floor; hot vertices are served from projections.
GRF.scaling: Sharded by source-node hash; multi-hop traversals are bounded and parallel across shards.
GRF.multiTenant: Edges never cross tenants implicitly; cross-tenant edges are explicit published relationships.
GRF.geo: Graph residency follows node sovereignty; replicas are read-only and policy-filtered.
GRF.failure: Hotspot overload, traversal timeout, edge-type drift, orphaned nodes.
GRF.recovery: The graph is rebuilt from the Relationship Domain's append-only log — it is a projection, never primary truth.
GRF.certification: Traversal must prove policy enforcement on every edge touched — no bypass, no post-filter leak.
GRF.migration: New edge types are registry additions; the graph re-indexes without downtime.
GRF.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller
    participant GR as Graph
    participant PL as Policy
    C->>GR: traverse(query, context)
    GR->>PL: edge access policy
    PL-->>GR: filter set
    GR->>GR: bounded traversal
    GR-->>C: results
```
GRF.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Parsing
    Parsing --> PolicyBinding
    PolicyBinding --> Traversing
    Traversing --> TrustWeighting
```
GRF.blueprint: Build order for GRF: (1) define registry entries — this domain owns by content: primitive-graph / projection-graph / meta-graph as registry truth, not code; (2) implement the contract surface first (graph.traverse, graph.neighbors, graph.path) and validate against GRF boundaries; (3) event-source all state so history is reconstructable; (4) wire the enforcement points — authority check, policy guard, evidence binding, trace — in-line, with no bypass path; (5) add tests per the Testing Architecture, citing evidence per gate; (6) obtain Verification and Certification before activation. Acceptance: the Zero Partial and Law 001 audits pass, every action answers the seven explainability questions, and this domain mutates no other domain internals.

IDX.concepts: Index Architecture makes the platform queryable at scale. Indexes are derived projections — rebuilt from truth, never authoritative — and their consistency with the source is continuously verified.
IDX.ontology: Index has a Source (domain truth), a Projection function, a Consistency model, and a Rebuild policy. An index that diverges from truth is a defect, not an optimization.
IDX.taxonomy: By structure: Inverted / B-tree / Hash / Graph / Vector / Hybrid. By consistency: Strong / Eventually / Snapshot. By trigger: Real-time / Batch / Scheduled.
IDX.dataModel:
```yaml
Index:
  indexId: <Identity>
  source: <domain partition>
  projectionFn: <registry expression>
  consistencyModel: <registry id>
  rebuildPolicy: <Policy>
  state: <Fresh|Stale|Rebuilding|Degraded>
  version: <int>
```
IDX.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Defined
    Defined --> Fresh
    Fresh --> Stale: source changed
    Stale --> Rebuilding
    Rebuilding --> Fresh
    Fresh --> Degraded: consistency violation
    Degraded --> Rebuilding
```
workflow: define projection → build → invalidate on source change → rebuild per policy → verify consistency
authorities: Index Authority (infrastructure); projection function must respect domain access contracts.
IDX.privacy: Indexes over personal data inherit consent scope at build time — no index of unseen data.
IDX.audit: Consistency verification is continuous; violations are events with source and index versions recorded.
IDX.twin: Index twin monitors lag and rebuild success rates across the fleet.
IDX.agent: Index agent detects query patterns and proposes new indexes, and flags unused ones for retirement.
IDX.runtime: Invalidation is event-driven from the source domain; queries to stale indexes are served with a staleness marker, never silently.
IDX.scaling: Indexes partition alongside their sources; rebuilds are incremental where the projection permits.
IDX.multiTenant: Indexes are tenant-scoped; a shared index over published data respects each source's policy.
IDX.geo: Indexes replicate for read locality; the authoritative build stays in the source's jurisdiction.
IDX.failure: Consistency violation, rebuild failure, invalidation storm, projection drift after schema evolution.
IDX.recovery: Indexes are disposable — a corrupt index is dropped and rebuilt from truth, never repaired in place.
IDX.certification: Index must carry a consistency guarantee level and prove verification runs on schedule.
IDX.migration: New index types are registry additions; schema evolution triggers governed rebuilds.
IDX.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant E as Source Event
    participant IX as Index
    participant TR as Truth
    E->>IX: source changed
    IX->>IX: invalidate
    IX->>TR: rebuild projection
    TR-->>IX: rebuilt
    IX->>IX: verify consistency
    IX-->>E: IndexRebuilt
```
IDX.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Building
    Building --> Fresh
    Fresh --> Invalidated
```

SRC.concepts: Search Architecture is context-aware discovery over projections. Search is not a feature bolted on — it is a governed query path respecting semantics, context policy, privacy, and perspective.
SRC.ontology: Search has a Query (semantic + context), a Ranking policy, a Filter set (context/perspective/privacy), and a Result provenance. Ranking is policy-driven; relevance is never the only criterion.
SRC.taxonomy: By modality: Keyword / Semantic / Faceted / Hybrid / Voice / Visual / Future. By scope: Tenant / Marketplace / Federated. By personalization: Universal / Segment / Individual (consent-gated).
SRC.dataModel:
```yaml
SearchQuery:
  queryId: <Identity>
  semanticConcept: <SemanticModel|null>
  context: <Context>
  filters: [<Policy>]
  rankingPolicy: <Policy>
  perspective: <Perspective>
  temporal: {at}
  personalizationScope: <consent scope|null>
```
SRC.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Parsing
    Parsing --> Disambiguating
    Disambiguated: note
    Disambiguating --> Filtering
    Filtering --> Ranking
    Ranking --> Serving
    Serving --> [*]
```
workflow: parse query → semantic disambiguation → context + privacy filtering → policy ranking → perspective projection → serve
authorities: Search Authority (infrastructure); ranking and filter policies carry their own authorities.
SRC.privacy: Personalization requires consent; without it, search is context-scoped only. Query logs are minimized and retention-bounded.
SRC.audit: Every search records context, filters applied, ranking policy version — required for marketplace fairness audit.
SRC.twin: Search twin monitors zero-result rates and latency as catalog-health signals.
SRC.agent: Search agent detects rising unmet queries and proposes catalog or semantic gaps to the owning domains.
SRC.runtime: Query planning fans out to indexes in parallel; results merge under ranking policy with consistent pagination.
SRC.scaling: Search scales with index partitioning; hot queries are cached with policy-version invalidation.
SRC.multiTenant: Search is tenant-scoped; marketplace search aggregates only published projections under marketplace policy.
SRC.geo: Search respects geo-context — availability, language, and compliance projected per region.
SRC.failure: Semantic ambiguity collapse, filter policy conflict, ranking bias, index staleness.
SRC.recovery: Search is stateless over truth — results recompute from indexes; caches are disposable.
SRC.certification: Search must prove filters were applied before ranking — privacy before relevance, always.
SRC.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller
    participant SE as Search
    participant IX as Index
    participant PL as Policy
    C->>SE: query(text, context)
    SE->>SE: semantic disambiguation
    SE->>IX: parallel fan-out
    IX-->>SE: candidates
    SE->>PL: filter + rank
    PL-->>SE: policy
    SE-->>C: results
```
SRC.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Understanding
    Understanding --> Filtering
    Filtering --> Ranking
    Ranking --> Projecting
```

CCH.concepts: Cache Architecture makes projections fast. Everything cached is derived and disposable — a cache is never a source of truth, and its consistency with the registry is a first-class concern.
CCH.ontology: Cache has a Key (content or semantic), a Source projection, an Invalidation policy, and a Consistency level. The invariant: a cache hit must be indistinguishable from recomputation under the pinned registry version.
CCH.taxonomy: By key: Content-addressed / Semantic / Query. By level: Request / Node / Cluster / Edge. By invalidation: Event-driven / TTL / Version-pinned / Hybrid.
CCH.dataModel:
```yaml
CacheEntry:
  cacheKey: <hash or semantic key>
  sourceProjection: <content-addressed>
  registryVersion: <version>
  invalidationPolicy: <Policy>
  consistency: <Strong|Eventually>
  temporal: {cachedAt, expiresAt}
  provenance: <computation ref>
```
CCH.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Empty
    Empty --> Filled: put
    Filled --> Valid
    Valid --> Stale: source changed
    Stale --> Empty: invalidated
    Valid --> Expired: TTL
    Expired --> Empty
```
workflow: compute key → check cache → on miss compute from registry → store with pinned version → invalidate on source event or TTL
authorities: Cache Authority (infrastructure); invalidation policy is governed per projection type.
CCH.privacy: Personal-data caches are consent-scoped and subject to erasure invalidation — a purge propagates to all caches.
CCH.audit: Consistency sampling proves cache matches recomputation; violations are events, not silent corrections.
CCH.twin: Cache twin monitors hit rates, eviction storms, and consistency-sample failures.
CCH.agent: Cache agent warms predicted-hot keys and identifies low-value entries for eviction.
CCH.runtime: Invalidation is event-driven from the source domains; edge caches are eventually consistent with staleness bounds.
CCH.scaling: Multi-tier: request → node → cluster → edge; each tier bounded by its invalidation latency.
CCH.multiTenant: Cache keys are tenant-namespaced — cross-tenant key collision is impossible by construction.
CCH.geo: Edge caches serve locality; regulated data's caches stay in-jurisdiction per residency policy.
CCH.failure: Stale-serve, invalidation loss, cache stampede, hot-key hotspot.
CCH.recovery: Caches are disposable — flush and recompute is always a safe recovery; no truth is ever cached-only.
CCH.certification: Cache must declare consistency level and prove invalidation latency within policy bound.
CCH.migration: New invalidation strategies are registry additions.
CCH.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller
    participant CH as Cache
    participant RG as Registry
    C->>CH: get(key)
    CH->>CH: lookup
    alt hit
        CH-->>C: value
    else miss
        CH->>RG: compute projection
        RG-->>CH: value
        CH->>CH: store pinned
        CH-->>C: value
    end
```
CCH.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Keying
    Keying --> Looking
    Looking --> Serving
    Looking --> Computing
    Computing --> Pinning
```
CCH.blueprint: Build order for CCH: (1) define registry entries — this domain owns by key: content-addressed / semantic / query as registry truth, not code; (2) implement the contract surface first (cache.put, cache.invalidate, cache.warm) and validate against CCH boundaries; (3) event-source all state so history is reconstructable; (4) wire the enforcement points — authority check, policy guard, evidence binding, trace — in-line, with no bypass path; (5) add tests per the Testing Architecture, citing evidence per gate; (6) obtain Verification and Certification before activation. Acceptance: the Zero Partial and Law 001 audits pass, every action answers the seven explainability questions, and this domain mutates no other domain internals.

EVT.concepts: Event Architecture is the platform's nervous system — every state change is an immutable, evidenced, well-schema'd event. Events are how domains communicate without coupling; they are the only legitimate cross-domain broadcast.
EVT.ontology: Event has a Type (registry), a Payload (schema-versioned), a Causation id, a Correlation id, an Authority, and Evidence. Events are facts that occurred — immutable once published.
EVT.taxonomy: By scope: Domain / Cross-domain / Platform / External. By delivery: At-least-once / Exactly-once (projected) / Best-effort. By tempo: Real-time / Batched / Scheduled.
EVT.dataModel:
```yaml
Event:
  eventId: <Identity>
  eventType: <registry id>
  schemaVersion: <version>
  payload: <schema-validated>
  causationId: <Event|null>
  correlationId: <Identity>
  authority: <Authority>
  evidence: <Evidence ref>
  temporal: {at}
  context: <Context>
```
EVT.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Produced
    Produced --> Validated
    Validated --> Published
    Published --> Delivered
    Delivered --> [*]
    Validated --> Rejected: schema invalid
```
workflow: produce → validate against registry schema → attach evidence + authority → publish → deliver to subscribers → retain per policy
authorities: Publishing domain's authority; subscribers verify, never trust.
EVT.privacy: Event payloads minimize personal data; sensitive types carry consent scope and are redactable in projections, never in the log itself.
EVT.audit: The event log is the audit spine — causation chains reconstruct any state of the system at any time.
EVT.twin: Event twin monitors throughput, schema-rejection rates, and subscriber lag as platform health.
EVT.agent: Event agents detect anomalies in event flows (drops, surges, schema drift) and alert.
EVT.runtime: At-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers; exactly-once is projected at the consumer via dedup keys.
EVT.scaling: Partition by event type + correlation hash; replay is a first-class operation for recovery.
EVT.multiTenant: Events are tenant-namespaced; cross-tenant subscription requires published relationship and policy.
EVT.geo: Event logs reside in the publishing domain's jurisdiction; cross-region replication respects residency.
EVT.failure: Schema rejection storm, subscriber lag, causation cycle, replay divergence.
EVT.recovery: Replay rebuilds any projection; the log is the recovery source. Compaction preserves causation, never facts.
EVT.certification: Event must carry schema version, authority, and evidence to be published — unverifiable events are rejected.
EVT.migration: New types are registry additions; schema evolution is versioned with backward-compatible readers.
EVT.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant D as Domain
    participant EB as Event Bus
    participant S as Subscriber
    D->>EB: publish(event)
    EB->>EB: schema + evidence validate
    EB->>S: deliver
    S->>S: idempotent apply
    S-->>EB: ack
```
EVT.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Producing
    Producing --> Validating
    Validating --> Publishing
    Publishing --> Delivering
```

Acceptance: the Zero Partial and Law 001 audits pass, every action answers the seven explainability questions, and this domain mutates no other domain internals.

MSG.concepts: Messaging Architecture provides reliable, contract-governed communication between domains, services, and external systems. Messaging is the point-to-point complement to events — directed, contracted, and confirmed.
MSG.ontology: Message has a Contract (registry), a Payload, a Delivery guarantee, and a Dead-letter path. Every queue is owned; every topic is governed; no anonymous producers or consumers exist.
MSG.taxonomy: By pattern: Queue / Topic / Stream / Request-reply. By guarantee: At-most-once / At-least-once / Exactly-once-projected. By scope: Intra-domain / Cross-domain / External.
MSG.dataModel:
```yaml
Message:
  messageId: <Identity>
  contractId: <registry contract>
  payload: <schema-validated>
  deliveryGuarantee: <registry id>
  authority: <Authority>
  temporal: {sentAt, deliveredAt}
  deadLetter: <DeadLetter ref|null>
```
MSG.stateMachine:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Sent
    Sent --> Delivered
    Delivered --> Acked
    Delivered --> Nacked
    Nacked --> Redelivered
    Nacked --> DeadLettered: retry exhausted
    Acked --> [*]
```
workflow: send under contract → validate schema → deliver → ack/nack → redeliver with backoff → dead-letter on exhaustion
authorities: Contract Authority (defines allowed interactions); producer and consumer domains each hold authority.
MSG.privacy: Personal-data messages are consent-scoped; dead-letters are purged per retention policy with evidence.
MSG.audit: Every message records contract version, authority, and delivery path — integration audit is complete.
MSG.twin: Messaging twin monitors depth, lag, and dead-letter rates across all contracts.
MSG.agent: Messaging agent detects contract drift and poison-message patterns, proposing contract fixes under governance.
MSG.runtime: Consumers are idempotent by contract requirement; backoff is exponential with jitter; dead-letters alert.
MSG.scaling: Partitions by contract; consumers scale per queue depth with policy bounds.
MSG.multiTenant: Queues are tenant-namespaced; cross-tenant messaging requires a published contract and both authorities.
MSG.geo: Cross-region messaging respects residency; external egress is policy-governed and audited.
MSG.failure: Poison message, contract violation, consumer starvation, dead-letter overflow.
MSG.recovery: Dead-letters are replayable after governed fix; acked messages are immutable facts.
MSG.certification: Contract must exist and both parties must be authorized — unsigned traffic is dropped at the edge.
MSG.migration: New contracts are registry additions; contract evolution is versioned with compatibility windows.
MSG.sequence:
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant P as Producer
    participant MQ as Messaging
    participant C as Consumer
    P->>MQ: send(contract, payload)
    MQ->>MQ: contract + schema validate
    MQ->>C: deliver
    C-->>MQ: ack
    MQ-->>P: delivered
```
MSG.state:
```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Contracting
    Contracting --> Validating
    Validating --> Delivering
    Delivering --> Settling
```
